question: An 18-year-old man presents to the student health department at his university for recurrent palpitations. The patient had previously presented to the emergency department (ED) for sudden onset palpitations five months ago when he first started college. He had a negative cardiac workup in the ED and he was discharged with a 24-hour Holter monitor which was also negative. He has no history of any medical or psychiatric illnesses. The patient reports that since his initial ED visit, he has had several episodes of unprovoked palpitations associated with feelings of dread and lightheadedness though he cannot identify a particular trigger. Recently, he has begun sitting towards the back of the lecture halls so that he can “quickly escape and not make a scene” in case he gets an episode in class. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Recurrent palpitations" -> "Negative cardiac workup in the emergency department" -> "Negative 24-hour Holter monitor" -> "No cardiac abnormalities detected" -> "Experiencing unprovoked palpitations associated with dread and lightheadedness" -> "Episodes of palpitations causing anticipatory anxiety" -> "Sitting towards the back of lecture halls to escape potential episodes" -> "Symptoms suggestive of panic attacks" -> "Likely diagnosis: Panic disorder" -> 85%

enhanced_information: The patient's presentation of recurrent palpitations, negative cardiac workup, unprovoked palpitations associated with dread and lightheadedness, anticipatory anxiety, and avoidance behavior in lecture halls suggest a likely diagnosis of panic disorder. The evidence paths do not provide additional relevant support for the diagnosis.
analysis: The patient's presentation of recurrent palpitations, negative cardiac workup, unprovoked palpitations associated with dread and lightheadedness, anticipatory anxiety, and avoidance behavior in lecture halls strongly suggest a diagnosis of panic disorder. Panic disorder is characterized by recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by at least one month of persistent concern about having another attack, worry about the implications of the attack, or a significant change in behavior related to the attacks. The patient's symptoms align well with the diagnostic criteria for panic disorder.
